solution:
**Primary sources** are sources that emit light of their own. They do so because of (i) their high temperature (the Sun, the stars, a flame, any object heated to a high temperature), (ii) the effect of a current passed through them (a tube light, a TV screen), or (iii) a chemical or nuclear reaction (firecrackers, nuclear energy generators). Light originates in these sources.

**Secondary sources** are sources that do not produce light of their own but receive light from some other source and either reflect or scatter it around. The moon, the planets, and ordinary objects such as humans, animals and plants are secondary sources -- we see them by the light they reflect.

Most of the sources we see in daily life are secondary sources, and most of them are **extended** sources rather than point sources.

**Wavefront.** The phase of a wave at a point is fixed by the state of motion of the particle at that point together with its distance from the source. A **wavefront is the locus of all points of the medium that have the same phase at a given instant** -- equivalently, the locus of all points that waves starting simultaneously from the source reach at the same instant.

**Relation to rays.** A ray of light is simply the direction in which the wave travels, and **the direction of propagation is always perpendicular (normal) to the wavefront**. So the rays are the normals to the wavefronts: for a point source the wavefronts are concentric spheres and the rays are the radii drawn outward from the source; for a parallel beam the wavefronts are parallel planes and the rays are parallel straight lines perpendicular to them. A ray diagram and a wavefront diagram carry the same information -- one drawn with lines along the propagation direction, the other with surfaces across it.

**Shape far from the source.** Close to a point source the wavefront is **spherical**. As the wave travels outward the radius of that sphere grows, so its curvature falls. At a large distance from the source any small portion of the wavefront that we actually observe is a tiny patch of a sphere of enormous radius, and it is indistinguishable from a flat surface -- just as the surface of the Earth appears flat to us. Hence **at a point far away from the source the wavefront is plane**, and the corresponding rays are parallel.

The colours are **not** due to any pigment in the oil. They are produced by the **interference of light waves reflected from the upper and the lower surface of the thin film**.

Refer to the diagram. Light incident at A on the top surface of the oil film (refractive index \( n_2 \), thickness \( d \)) is **partly reflected** there, along AE. The rest is refracted into the film and travels to B on the lower surface, where it is again partly reflected along BC, and at C it refracts back out into the air along CF.

The two emerging rays **AE and CF are parallel and are derived from the same incident wave, so they are coherent** and they interfere. They have travelled different paths -- one of them has made an extra journey down and back up through the film -- so there is a path difference between them. Two further points decide the result:

- The path difference depends on the **thickness \( d \)** of the film at the point being viewed and on the **angle of incidence \( \theta_1 \)**, which is the angle at which you are looking at the film.
- It also depends on the **wavelength**, both directly and because the refractive index of the oil itself depends on wavelength.
- Because the reflection at A is at the surface of a **denser** medium, that ray suffers an additional phase difference of \( \pi \) radians, i.e. an extra path difference of \( \lambda/2 \), which must be included in any calculation.

White light contains all wavelengths at once. At a given thickness and a given viewing angle the path difference works out to a whole number of wavelengths for **one** colour (constructive interference, so that colour is strong) while for another colour it is an odd number of half wavelengths (destructive interference, so that colour is missing). Since the film thickness varies from point to point and the viewing angle varies across the film, a **different colour is reinforced at each point and at each angle** -- which is why the oil film shows a shifting pattern of multiple colours, and why the colours change as you move your head. The brilliant colours of soap bubbles have exactly the same origin.

**No interference pattern will be seen.** The screen will show only the general overlap of red light and violet light -- a patch of illumination, with no bright and dark fringes at all.

**Reason.** For a sustained interference pattern the two sources must be **coherent**, and coherent sources are defined as two sources that emit waves of the **same frequency** with a **constant phase difference** between them, independent of time. With a red filter over one slit and a violet filter over the other, the two slits emit light of two quite different frequencies. Two waves of different frequency cannot maintain a constant phase difference: their relative phase runs through every value continuously, so the positions of maxima and minima would change from instant to instant and nothing steady is produced.

There is a second, independent reason. Even if one tried to treat the two colours separately, the fringe positions and the fringe width \( W = \lambda D/d \) both depend on the wavelength, so the red pattern and the violet pattern would not be coincident. But the decisive point is the first one -- with only one wavelength arriving at each slit there is no pair of coherent sources at all, so neither pattern is produced.

This is why the two secondary sources in an interference experiment are always derived from **one** original source, and why the light used must be monochromatic.

**Optical path length.** When a wave travels a distance \( \Delta x \) through a medium of refractive index \( n \), its speed there is \( v = c/n \) and its phase changes by
\( \Delta \phi' = \dfrac{\omega n \Delta x}{c}. \)
That is exactly the phase change the same wave would have acquired had it travelled a distance \( n\,\Delta x \) **in vacuum**. This equivalent distance is called the **optical path**:
\( \text{optical path} = n \times (\text{actual path in the medium}). \)
Equivalently, the optical path in a medium is the distance the light would cover **in vacuum in the same time** it actually takes in the medium.

**How it differs from the actual path length.** The actual (geometrical) path length is simply the physical distance the light covers. The optical path is that distance multiplied by the refractive index, so:

- In **vacuum** \( n = 1 \) and the two are equal.
- In any material medium \( n > 1 \), so the **optical path is always longer than the actual path**, even though the light physically covers the shorter distance.
- The actual path is what a ruler measures; the optical path is what the **phase** measures. Interference is decided by phase, so it is optical path -- not actual path -- that must be compared. Two waves interfere constructively when their optical path lengths are equal or differ by an integral multiple of \( \lambda \).

For example, a transparent plate of thickness \( t \) and refractive index \( n \) placed in the way of one beam adds an extra optical path of \( nt - t = (n-1)t \) relative to a beam travelling the same geometrical distance through vacuum, and it is this extra \( (n-1)t \) that shifts the whole interference pattern to one side.

**Laws of reflection from Huygens' principle.**

Let a plane wavefront AB, perpendicular to the plane of the paper, be incident at an angle \( i \) on a plane reflecting surface MN, also perpendicular to the paper. RA and QB show the direction of incidence.

**Set-up.** Let the incident wavefront touch the surface at A at time \( t = 0 \). The other end B of the wavefront travels on and reaches the surface at C after a time \( t = T \). Between \( t = 0 \) and \( t = T \) the intermediate points of the wavefront strike the surface one after another, and by Huygens' principle each becomes a secondary source sending out hemispherical wavelets. For reflection the hemispheres to be considered lie on the **same** side of the mirror.

**The reflected wavefront.** Both the wavelet from A and the incident wave travel in the same medium with the same speed \( v \), so in the time \( T \):
\( \text{AE} = \text{BC} = vT. \)
The wavelet from A has grown to radius \( vT \) by time \( T \); the wavelet just starting at C has radius zero; the wavelets from the points between A and C have radii decreasing steadily from \( vT \) to \( 0 \). The **envelope** of all of them is the straight line EC, which is therefore the **reflected wavefront**, and AE gives the direction of the reflected wave.

**First law -- angle of incidence equals angle of reflection.** AP is the normal to MN at A, so the angle of incidence is \( \angle \text{RAP} = i \). Since RA is perpendicular to the wavefront AB and AP is perpendicular to the surface AC,
\( \angle \text{BAC} = i. \)
Now compare triangles \( \Delta \text{ABC} \) and \( \Delta \text{AEC} \). Both are right angled, they have the **common hypotenuse AC**, and one pair of equal sides, \( \text{AE} = \text{BC} = vT \). Hence the two triangles are congruent, giving
\( \angle \text{ACE} = \angle \text{BAC} = i. \qquad \cdots (1) \)
The angle of reflection is \( \angle \text{PAE} = r \). Because AE is perpendicular to CE and AP is perpendicular to AC,
\( \angle \text{ACE} = \angle \text{PAE} = r. \qquad \cdots (2) \)
From (1) and (2),
\( \boxed{\, i = r \,} \)
**the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection** -- the first law of reflection.

**Second law -- the three lie in one plane.** It is clear from the construction that the incident ray, the normal AP and the reflected ray all lie in the plane of the paper, i.e. **the incident ray, the reflected ray and the normal to the surface at the point of incidence all lie in the same plane**. This is the second law of reflection.

Both laws therefore follow from Huygens' construction alone, with no assumption beyond the wave nature of light.

**Laws of refraction (Snell's law) from Huygens' principle.**

Consider a plane wavefront AB incident on a plane boundary MN separating two uniform transparent media, of absolute refractive indices \( n_1 \) (medium 1, above) and \( n_2 \) (medium 2, below). Let the speed of light be \( v_1 \) in medium 1 and \( v_2 \) in medium 2.

**Set-up.** At time \( t = 0 \) the end A of the wavefront has just reached the boundary, while the other end B still has to travel; B reaches the boundary at C at a later time \( t = T \). In medium 1 that journey covers
\( \text{BC} = v_1 T. \)
Meanwhile, by Huygens' principle A has become a secondary source and has been sending wavelets **into medium 2**, where they travel with speed \( v_2 \). At time \( T \) the wavelet from A has therefore grown to a radius
\( \text{AE} = v_2 T. \)
The intermediate points between A and C start their wavelets at intermediate times, so their radii decrease steadily from \( v_2 T \) to zero. The **refracted wavefront** is the envelope of all these wavelets, i.e. the common tangent CE.

**Deriving the relation.** Let PP' be the normal to the boundary at A. Then
\( \angle \text{A}'\text{AP} = \angle \text{BAC} = i \quad (\text{the angle of incidence}), \)
\( \angle \text{P}'\text{AE} = \angle \text{ACE} = r \quad (\text{the angle of refraction}). \)
From the right angled triangle \( \Delta \text{ABC} \):
\( \sin i = \dfrac{\text{BC}}{\text{AC}} = \dfrac{v_1 T}{\text{AC}}. \qquad \cdots (1) \)
From the right angled triangle \( \Delta \text{AEC} \):
\( \sin r = \dfrac{\text{AE}}{\text{AC}} = \dfrac{v_2 T}{\text{AC}}. \qquad \cdots (2) \)
Dividing (1) by (2), the common factors \( T \) and AC cancel:
\( \dfrac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \dfrac{v_1}{v_2} = \dfrac{c/n_1}{c/n_2} = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}, \)
using \( v = c/n \). Hence
\( \boxed{\, n_1 \sin i = n_2 \sin r \,} \)
which is **Snell's law**, the first law of refraction. The ratio \( \sin i / \sin r \) is a constant for a given pair of media, since \( n_1 \) and \( n_2 \) are constants.

**Second law.** From the construction the incident ray, the refracted ray and the normal to the boundary all lie in the plane of the paper, i.e. **in the same plane** -- the second law of refraction.

**Bending.** If \( v_1 > v_2 \), i.e. \( n_1 < n_2 \), then \( i > r \): going from an optically rarer to an optically denser medium the refracted ray bends **towards** the normal. Going from a denser to a rarer medium it bends **away** from the normal.

**Polarization.**

Light is a transverse electromagnetic wave: for a wave travelling along the \( x \)-axis the electric field lies somewhere in the \( y \)-\( z \) plane, perpendicular to the direction of propagation. Different atoms of an ordinary source emit independently, so the electric fields of the waves coming from a bulb or the Sun point in **all possible directions** in that perpendicular plane. Such light is called **unpolarized** light.

If light is constrained so that its **electric field is restricted to one particular direction**, it is called **plane polarized** (linearly polarized) light, and this restriction is what is meant by **polarization**. Materials that transmit only those waves whose electric field lies along one particular direction are called **polarizers**; a polaroid is a synthetic plastic sheet used as one. The direction along which the transmitted electric field is oriented is the **polarizing axis**. The plane containing the electric field vectors of the polarized light is the *plane of vibration*, and the plane perpendicular to it is the *plane of polarization*.

Only **transverse** waves can be polarized. A longitudinal wave (sound, for instance) oscillates only along its direction of propagation, so there is nothing to restrict.

**Intensity after the first polarizer.** Consider a particular wave whose electric field makes an angle \( \phi \) with the axis of the first polarizer. The component \( E_0 \cos\phi \) is transmitted and the perpendicular component \( E_0 \sin\phi \) is blocked, so the transmitted intensity of that one wave is proportional to \( |E_0 \cos\phi|^2 \). For **unpolarized** incident light \( \phi \) takes every value from \( 0 \) to \( 180^\circ \), so we must average \( \cos^2\phi \) over that range. Since the average of \( \cos^2\phi \) is \( 1/2 \), the emergent intensity is proportional to \( \tfrac{1}{2}|E_0|^2 \):
\( I_1 = \dfrac{I_0}{2}. \)
**The intensity of unpolarized light is halved on passing through a polarizer**, whatever the orientation of its axis.

**Derivation of Malus' law.** The light leaving the first polarizer is linearly polarized. Let its electric field be along the \( y \)-direction,
\( \vec{E_1} = \hat{j}\, E_{10} \sin(kx - \omega t), \qquad I_1 \propto |E_{10}|^2. \)
Let it now fall on a second polarizer whose polarizing axis makes an angle \( \theta \) with the \( y \)-direction, i.e. with the axis of the first. Only the component of \( \vec{E_1} \) **along that axis** can pass, so the transmitted amplitude is
\( E_{20} = E_{10} \cos\theta. \)
The intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude, so
\( I_2 \propto |E_{20}|^2 = |E_{10}|^2 \cos^2\theta, \)
\( \boxed{\, I_2 = I_1 \cos^2\theta \,} \)
This is **Malus' law**: it gives the intensity of a linearly polarized wave after it passes through a polarizer, \( \theta \) being the angle between the **axes of polarization of the two polarizers**.

**Checks.** If \( \theta = 0 \) the axes are parallel, \( \cos^2\theta = 1 \) and the intensity is unchanged (the *parallel* setting). If \( \theta = 90^\circ \), \( \cos^2\theta = 0 \) and no light emerges at all (the *cross* setting).

**Brewster's law.**

When light is incident at an angle on the boundary between two transparent media of refractive indices \( n_1 \) and \( n_2 \), part of it is refracted and the rest reflected. In general both the reflected and the refracted beams are only **partially** polarized. D. Brewster discovered experimentally in 1812 that **there is one particular angle of incidence, \( \theta_B \), at which the reflected wave is completely plane polarized**, its electric field being perpendicular to the plane of the paper (the plane of incidence), while the refracted wave remains partially polarized. This angle is called the **Brewster angle** or the polarizing angle.

**Statement.** Brewster's law states that the tangent of the polarizing angle equals the refractive index of the second medium with respect to the first:
\( \tan\theta_B = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}. \)

**Derivation of the formula.** The key observation is that **at the Brewster angle the reflected ray and the refracted ray are perpendicular to each other**. If \( \theta_r \) is the angle of refraction, then from the geometry of the figure (the reflected ray makes an angle \( \theta_B \) with the normal on one side and the refracted ray makes \( \theta_r \) on the other, and the angle between them is \( 90^\circ \)):
\( \theta_B + \theta_r = 90^\circ, \qquad \text{so} \qquad \theta_r = 90^\circ - \theta_B. \qquad \cdots (1) \)
Applying the law of refraction (Snell's law) at the boundary,
\( n_1 \sin\theta_B = n_2 \sin\theta_r. \qquad \cdots (2) \)
Substituting (1) into (2),
\( n_1 \sin\theta_B = n_2 \sin(90^\circ - \theta_B) = n_2 \cos\theta_B. \)
Dividing both sides by \( n_1 \cos\theta_B \),
\( \dfrac{\sin\theta_B}{\cos\theta_B} = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}, \qquad \text{i.e.} \qquad \tan\theta_B = \dfrac{n_2}{n_1}, \)
\( \boxed{\; \theta_B = \tan^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac{n_2}{n_1}\right) \;} \)
which is the required formula for the Brewster angle. For light incident from air (\( n_1 = 1 \)) onto a medium of refractive index \( n \), this reduces to \( \theta_B = \tan^{-1}(n) \).

**Application.** Polarization by reflection is what allows polaroid sunglasses to cut glare: light reflected from a road, water or glass is strongly polarized, so a polaroid with its axis set to block that direction removes most of it. Note that the phenomenon works only for **non-metallic** surfaces.

**Young's double slit experiment.**

**The arrangement.** A plane wavefront is made to fall on an opaque screen AB carrying two similar narrow slits \( S_1 \) and \( S_2 \). The plane wavefront is obtained either by placing a linear source S far away from AB, or by placing S at the focus of a convex lens kept close to AB so that the rays emerging from the lens are parallel. For good results the slits should be about 2--4 mm apart. An observing screen PQ is placed behind AB, at a distance \( D \) which should be about a metre. \( S_1 \) and \( S_2 \) are equidistant from S, so the wavefronts reaching them are always in phase.

When the wave reaches \( S_1 \) and \( S_2 \), by Huygens' principle **the two slits act as secondary sources** emitting cylindrical wavelets. Since they are derived from a single primary source they emit **in phase at all times, i.e. they are coherent**, and the two sets of wavelets superpose in the region beyond AB. Where crest falls on crest the interference is constructive and the screen is bright; where crest falls on trough it is destructive and the screen is dark. The alternate bright and dark regions are the **fringes** and the whole pattern is the **interference pattern**.

**Geometry.** Take the direction of propagation as the \( x \)-axis and let the screen lie in the \( y \)-\( z \) plane. Let O be the mid-point of \( S_1 S_2 \), let the slit separation be \( d \), and let the distance from the slits to the screen be \( D \). O' is the point on the screen level with O, so \( S_1 \text{O}' = S_2 \text{O}' \): the two waves arrive at O' in phase and there is always a **bright fringe at the centre** of the screen.

**Path difference at a general point.** Let P be a point on the screen at a distance \( y \) from O'. Considering the two right triangles,
\( (S_2 P)^2 - (S_1 P)^2 = \left[D^2 + \left(y + \tfrac{d}{2}\right)^2\right] - \left[D^2 + \left(y - \tfrac{d}{2}\right)^2\right] = 2yd, \)
so
\( \Delta l = S_2 P - S_1 P = \dfrac{2yd}{S_2 P + S_1 P}. \)
Since \( d/D \ll 1 \) we may put \( S_2 P + S_1 P \approx 2D \), giving the standard result
\( \Delta l = \dfrac{2yd}{2D} = y\,\dfrac{d}{D}. \)

**Condition for a BRIGHT fringe.** The two waves reinforce when the path difference is a whole number of wavelengths:
\( \Delta l = y_n \dfrac{d}{D} = n\lambda, \qquad n = 0, \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots \)
so the \( n^{\text{th}} \) bright fringe is at
\( \boxed{\; y_n = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d} \;} \)
\( n = 0 \) is the **central** bright fringe (the zeroth, not the first).

**Condition for a DARK fringe.** The two waves cancel when the path difference is an odd number of half wavelengths:
\( \Delta l = y_n \dfrac{d}{D} = \left(n - \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\lambda, \qquad n = \pm 1, \pm 2, \ldots \)
so the \( n^{\text{th}} \) dark fringe is at
\( \boxed{\; y_n = \left(n - \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\dfrac{\lambda D}{d} \;} \)

**Fringe width.** The **fringe width \( W \) is defined as the distance between the centres of any two consecutive bright fringes, or equally of any two consecutive dark fringes.** Taking two successive bright fringes,
\( W = \Delta y = y_{n+1} - y_n = \dfrac{(n+1)\lambda D}{d} - \dfrac{n\lambda D}{d}, \)
\( \boxed{\; W = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} \;} \)
The same result follows from two successive dark fringes, so the bright and dark fringes are **equidistant and of equal width**. \( W \) is independent of \( n \), which is why the fringes are equally spaced; it increases with wavelength and with \( D \), and decreases as the slit separation \( d \) is made larger.

For the interference pattern to be **steady and clearly visible**, the following conditions must be satisfied.

**1. The two sources of light must be coherent.** This is the essential condition for a sustained pattern. Waves from coherent sources are always in phase, or keep a constant phase difference, at all times. If the phase difference varied with time, the positions of the maxima and minima would move with it and the pattern would not be steady -- which is why the two secondary sources are always derived from a single original source.

**2. The two sources must be monochromatic.** The positions of the fringes and the fringe width \( W = \lambda D/d \) both depend on the wavelength, so with white light the patterns of the different colours are not coincident and the result is a set of coloured, overlapping bands instead of clean fringes. (Young's original experiment did use sunlight and pinholes, and gave a coloured pattern with a white centre.)

**3. The two interfering waves must have the same amplitude.** Only when the amplitudes are equal is the intensity at the dark fringes exactly **zero**; the contrast between bright and dark is then a maximum. If the amplitudes differ, the minima are proportional to \( |E_{10} - E_{20}|^2 \), which is not zero, and the dark fringes are only partly dark.

**4. The separation between the two slits must be small compared with the distance from the slits to the screen (\( D \gg d \)).** Since \( W = \lambda D/d \), this is what makes the fringe width large enough to be measurable and the fringes well separated and clearly seen. It is also the approximation used in deriving the fringe positions.

**5. The two slits should be narrow.** If the slits are broad, the distances from different points of the *same* slit to a given point on the screen differ appreciably, so waves coming through one slit interfere among themselves; the result is a blurred pattern of poor contrast.

**6. The two waves should be in the same state of polarization.** This matters only if polarized light is used for the experiment. Waves polarized perpendicular to each other cannot produce cancellation.

**Coherent sources.** Two sources are said to be **coherent** if they emit waves of the **same frequency** with a **constant phase difference** between them that does not change with time.

Light waves from many sources overlap everywhere around us, so in principle they should interfere everywhere -- yet we never see an interference pattern in a room. The reason is that two independent sources emit at different frequencies, and even when the frequencies match the two are not in phase and their phase relation changes continuously. The positions of the maxima and minima therefore shift from instant to instant and no pattern is sustained long enough to be seen. Two independent **primary** sources can never satisfy the coherence criterion, because their atoms radiate independently.

**How coherence is achieved in the laboratory.** The way round this is not to use two independent sources at all, but to take light from **one** source and split it into two, so that any phase fluctuation of the original source affects both beams identically and the difference between them stays fixed. The two beams then act as two coherent **secondary** sources. Young's double slit experiment does exactly this, by passing light from a single source through two narrow slits. Two other standard laboratory methods are:

**(i) Lloyd's mirror.** Light from a source is allowed to fall at a **grazing angle** on a plane mirror. Part of the light travels directly to the screen; the rest reaches the screen after reflection from the mirror. The reflected light appears to come from a **virtual source** behind the mirror, so we have two sources -- the real one and its virtual image. Both are derived from a single original source, hence they are coherent, and they interfere to give a pattern on the screen in the region where the direct and reflected beams overlap.

**(ii) Fresnel biprism.** A biprism is a prism with a vertex angle of nearly \( 180^\circ \); it may be regarded as two prisms of very small refracting angle (between \( 30' \) and \( 1^\circ \)) joined at their bases. Monochromatic light from a narrow slit S is made to fall on the biprism, whose refracting edge is kept parallel to the length of the slit. The two halves of the biprism **refract the light through slightly different directions and so form two virtual images \( S_1 \) and \( S_2 \)** of the single slit. These two virtual images are the coherent sources; in the region where the two refracted beams overlap (the superposition region) they interfere and produce fringes just like those of Young's double slit experiment.

**Diffraction of light.** Geometrical optics rests on the rectilinear propagation of light -- light travels in straight lines and casts sharp shadows. In certain experiments, however, light is seen to **bend round the edges of an obstacle in its path and enter the region where a shadow was expected**. This bending of light round obstacles is the phenomenon of **diffraction**. It is common to all waves; we are familiar with it in sound, which travels round a wall so that we can hear a person we cannot see. Diffraction of sound is easier to observe because the wavelength of sound is much larger.

Strictly, light does not "bend" at the edge. It reaches the shadow region because, by Huygens' principle, **every point of the wavefront at the edge of the obstacle acts as a secondary source** and radiates wavelets in all directions. Diffraction is noticeable only when the size of the obstacle or the slit is **of the order of the wavelength of light**, which is why we rarely see it with everyday objects.

**How diffraction differs from interference.** Diffraction is intimately related to interference -- it *is* interference -- but the two differ in an important respect:

| Point of difference | Interference (two slits) | Diffraction (single slit) |
|---|---|---|
| Origin | superposition of waves from **two** separate coherent sources (the two slits) | superposition of the **many** secondary wavelets originating from different points of the **same** wavefront |
| Number of waves | essentially two | a very large number |
| Fringe width | \( W = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} \), \( d \) = slit separation | \( W = \dfrac{\lambda D}{a} \), \( a \) = slit width (except for the central fringe) |
| Bright fringe, path difference | \( n\lambda \) | \( \left(n + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\lambda \) |
| Dark fringe, path difference | \( \left(n - \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\lambda \) | \( n\lambda \) |
| Intensity of the fringes | all bright fringes are of **nearly the same** brightness | the **central** fringe is by far the brightest and is twice as wide; the others fall off rapidly |
| Number of fringes seen | about 30 to 40 | about 20 to 30 |

Note in particular that **the bright and dark conditions are interchanged** between the two: a path difference of \( n\lambda \) between the extreme rays gives a bright fringe in two-slit interference but a **dark** one in single-slit diffraction.

**Fraunhofer and Fresnel diffraction.** Diffraction is classified into two types according to the distances involved in the set-up:

**1. Fraunhofer diffraction.** The distances between the primary source, the diffracting obstacle or slit, and the screen are **very large**. The wavefront incident on the obstacle can then be taken to be a **plane** wavefront. In practice this is arranged by placing the source at the focus of a convex lens, and a second convex lens is used on the other side of the obstacle to bring the pattern to a focus on the screen.

**2. Fresnel diffraction.** The distances involved are **much smaller**, and the incident wavefront is **cylindrical or spherical** depending on the source. No lens is required to observe the pattern on the screen.

**Fraunhofer diffraction at a single slit -- conditions for dark and bright fringes.**

Let a plane wavefront YY' be incident normally on a single slit AB of width \( a \), with O the centre of the slit and the slit length perpendicular to the plane of the paper. A cylindrical lens beyond the slit focuses the emergent beams on a screen at its focus, so the screen distance \( D \) is essentially the focal length. For real set-ups \( a \sim 10^{-4} \) to \( 10^{-3} \) m while \( D \sim 10 \) m, so \( D \gg a \).

By Huygens' principle the slit may be imagined divided into a very large number of thin slit elements, **each of which becomes a secondary source** radiating in all directions. The pattern on the screen is the result of the interference of all these wavelets.

**The central maximum.** All the rays leaving the slit **parallel to the axis**, from every point between A and B, are focused at the central point \( P_0 \) directly in front of O. They all have equal optical paths, so they arrive with the **same phase** and interfere constructively. \( P_0 \) is therefore a bright point -- the central maximum.

**Condition for a DARK fringe (minimum).** Consider the rays leaving the slit at an angle \( \theta \) and focused at a point P. Drop AC normal to the ray direction; from AC onward there is no further path difference, so the whole path difference is generated between AB and AC. The path difference between the **extreme** rays (from A and from B) is
\( \text{BC} = a \sin\theta. \)
Suppose this equals \( \lambda \). Let K be the mid-point of AC, so \( \text{OK} = \tfrac{1}{2}\text{BC} = \lambda/2 \): the ray from A and the ray from O reach P with a path difference of \( \lambda/2 \) and therefore **cancel**. Now take *any* pair of points separated by \( a/2 \) along the slit -- G and H, say, or O and B. Every such pair has a path difference of \( \lambda/2 \) at P and so cancels. Since the whole slit can be divided into such pairs, one from AO and its partner from OB, **the contributions cancel in pairs and P is completely dark**. Extending the argument to path differences \( 2\lambda, 3\lambda, \ldots, n\lambda \), the condition for the \( n^{\text{th}} \) **dark** fringe is
\( \boxed{\; a \sin\theta = \pm\, n\lambda, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots \;} \)
(\( n = 0 \) is excluded -- it is the central *maximum*.)

**Condition for a BRIGHT fringe (secondary maximum).** The secondary maxima lie in between the successive minima. Taking them to be midway, the path difference between the extreme rays at the \( n^{\text{th}} \) maximum is an odd number of half wavelengths:
\( \boxed{\; a \sin\theta = \pm\left(n + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\lambda, \qquad n = 1, 2, 3, \ldots \;} \)
(In reality these maxima are *nearly*, not exactly, midway between the dark fringes.)

**Positions on the screen.** Since \( D \gg a \) the angle \( \theta \) is very small, so with \( y \) the distance of the point from the central bright point,
\( \sin\theta \approx \tan\theta \approx \theta = \dfrac{y}{D}. \)
Hence the \( n^{\text{th}} \) dark point is at
\( y_{nd} = \dfrac{n\lambda D}{a} = nW, \qquad \text{where } W = \dfrac{\lambda D}{a}, \)
and the \( n^{\text{th}} \) bright point at
\( y_{nb} \approx \left(n + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)\dfrac{\lambda D}{a} = \left(n + \tfrac{1}{2}\right)W. \)
\( W = \lambda D / a \) plays the role of the fringe width and is the spacing of consecutive bright (or dark) fringes, **except for the central bright fringe**.

**Width of the central bright fringe.** The central fringe is spread between the first dark fringes on either side, so
\( W_c = 2 y_{1d} = 2W = \dfrac{2\lambda D}{a}, \)
i.e. **the central maximum is twice as wide as any of the others** -- and it is also by far the brightest.

Note the contrast with two-slit interference, where \( n\lambda \) is the condition for a **bright** fringe: in single-slit diffraction \( n\lambda \) gives a **dark** one.

**Resolving power and Rayleigh's criterion.**

We use an optical instrument not merely to magnify but to **see distinct images of nearby objects**. The ability of an instrument to distinguish two physically separated objects as two distinct objects is called its **resolving power**. If a friend holds up two fingers 10 m away you can easily see that there are two; at 50 m most people cannot tell whether it is two fingers or one. The eye has ceased to *resolve* them.

The resolving ability is stated in terms of the **visual angle** subtended at the instrument by the two objects (taken to be point objects). The **minimum** angle at which two objects can still be told apart is the **limit of resolution**, and the **resolving power is the reciprocal of the limit of resolution**. It depends on the aperture (usually the diameter of the lens or mirror) and on the wavelength of the light used.

**Rayleigh's criterion.** Every point object, viewed through an aperture, produces not a point image but a **diffraction pattern** -- a bright central disc with fainter rings around it. According to Lord Rayleigh, two objects are **just resolved when the first minimum of the diffraction pattern of one source coincides with the central maximum of the diffraction pattern of the other, and vice versa.** In that situation there is a just-noticeable dip in the resultant envelope of the two patterns, and the eye reads it as two objects rather than one. If the objects are closer the dip is not noticeable and the two are **unresolved**; if they are farther apart the dip is obvious and they are **well resolved**.

**(a) Resolving power of a telescope.** A telescope is used on distant stars, which behave as luminous point objects, so their diffraction patterns are Airy discs and only the **angular** separation matters. Let the objective AB have aperture (diameter) \( D \), and let the two distant objects have angular separation \( \theta \). Applying Airy's theory to the Fraunhofer diffraction of a pair of point objects, the path difference between the extreme rays at the first dark ring is \( 1.22\lambda \):
\( BI' - AI' = 1.22\lambda. \)
For just resolution this must equal \( D \times \theta \), so
\( D\theta = 1.22\lambda, \qquad \boxed{\; \theta = \dfrac{1.22\,\lambda}{D} \;} \)
and the resolving power is
\( R = \dfrac{1}{\theta} = \dfrac{D}{1.22\,\lambda}. \)
Thus, for a given wavelength, **the objective of a telescope should be made as large as possible** for high resolving power. (Very large lenses bring aberrations and weight problems, so front-coated parabolic mirrors, often segmented, are preferred. Radio telescopes need apertures of kilometres, which is why arrays such as the GMRT are used.)

**(b) Resolving power of a microscope.** A microscope views nearby objects, so here the relevant quantity is the **least distance \( a \) between two points that can still be resolved**. For a pair of self-luminous point objects, the path difference between the extreme rays at the first dark ring is again \( 1.22\lambda_n \), where \( \lambda_n = \lambda/n \) is the wavelength in the medium filling the object space and \( \alpha \) is the half angle subtended by the objective at the object. The just-resolution requirement \( 2a\sin\alpha = 1.22\lambda_n \) gives
\( \boxed{\; a = \dfrac{1.22\,\lambda}{2n\sin\alpha} = \dfrac{0.61\,\lambda}{n \sin\alpha} = \dfrac{0.61\,\lambda}{(\text{N.A.})} \;} \)
where \( \text{N.A.} = n\sin\alpha \) is the **numerical aperture**. The resolving power is
\( R = \dfrac{1}{a} = \dfrac{(\text{N.A.})}{0.61\,\lambda}. \)
For better resolution \( a \) should be as **small** as possible, so a microscope should have a large numerical aperture and use a short wavelength. A large N.A. is obtained by using an **oil-immersion objective**, since the oil provides a higher value of \( n \).

**Summary of the difference.** For a telescope the limit is an **angle**, improved by enlarging the aperture; for a microscope it is a **distance**, improved by raising the numerical aperture and shortening the wavelength.

**Given:** wavelength range in air (vacuum) \( \lambda_{\text{air}} = 400 \) nm to \( 700 \) nm; refractive index of glass \( n = 1.55 \).

**Principle.** When light passes from air into a medium its **frequency does not change** -- the frequency is fixed by the source, and the number of waves arriving at the boundary per second must equal the number leaving. The speed falls to \( v = c/n \), so the wavelength must fall in the same ratio:
\( \lambda_{\text{medium}} = \dfrac{v}{\nu} = \dfrac{c/n}{\nu} = \dfrac{\lambda_{\text{air}}}{n}. \)

**Shorter end of the range.**
\( \lambda_1 = \dfrac{400}{1.55} = 258.06 \approx 258.1 \text{ nm} \)

**Longer end of the range.**
\( \lambda_2 = \dfrac{700}{1.55} = 451.61 \approx 451.6 \text{ nm} \)

**Answer:** inside the glass the wavelengths run from about \( 258.1 \) nm to \( 451.6 \) nm.

**Note on what is actually "seen".** Every wavelength is **reduced** by the factor \( 1/n \), so the whole band shrinks. But because the *frequency* is unchanged, the **colours perceived are the same as in air** -- violet is still seen as violet, even though its wavelength inside the glass is 258 nm rather than 400 nm. The colour of light is determined by its frequency, not by its wavelength in whatever medium it happens to be travelling.

**Given:** in flint glass, \( n_1 = 1.6 \) over an actual distance \( d_1 = 3 \) cm; in the second medium, \( n_2 = 1.25 \) over an actual distance \( d_2 = x \) cm. The two **optical paths** are equal.

**Principle.** The optical path through a medium is
\( \text{optical path} = n \times (\text{actual path}). \)

**Setting the two optical paths equal.**
\( n_1 d_1 = n_2 d_2 \)
\( 1.6 \times 3 = 1.25 \times x \)
\( 4.8 = 1.25\,x \)
\( x = \dfrac{4.8}{1.25} = 3.84 \)

**Answer:** \( x = 3.84 \) cm.

**Check for sense.** The second medium is optically **rarer** (\( 1.25 < 1.6 \)), so light must travel a **longer** geometrical distance in it to accumulate the same phase change -- and indeed \( 3.84 \) cm \( > 3 \) cm, as required.

**Given:** sodium light, \( \lambda = 589 \) nm in air; angular fringe separation in air \( \theta_{\text{air}} = 0.20^\circ \); the whole arrangement is then immersed in water, \( n = 1.33 \).

**Principle.** The \( n^{\text{th}} \) bright fringe lies at \( y_n = n\lambda D/d \), so the **angular** position is \( \theta_n = y_n/D = n\lambda/d \), and the **angular fringe separation** -- the angle between two consecutive fringes -- is
\( \theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{d}. \)
This depends on the wavelength but **not** on \( D \), which is why the answer does not need the screen distance.

**Effect of the water.** Immersing the apparatus does not change the slit separation \( d \), but the wavelength in water is
\( \lambda_w = \dfrac{\lambda}{n}. \)
Hence
\( \theta_w = \dfrac{\lambda_w}{d} = \dfrac{\lambda}{n\,d} = \dfrac{\theta_{\text{air}}}{n}. \)

**Substituting.**
\( \theta_w = \dfrac{0.20^\circ}{1.33} = 0.1504^\circ \approx 0.15^\circ \)

**Answer:** the angular fringe separation becomes about \( 0.15^\circ \).

Note the **direction of the change**: immersing the apparatus in water **decreases** the angular separation (the fringes crowd together), because the wavelength inside the water is shorter than in air. The given wavelength 589 nm is not needed numerically -- only the ratio matters.

**Given:** slit separation \( d = 100\lambda \); screen distance \( D = 50.0 \) cm \( = 0.500 \) m. The question asks about the central maximum and the maximum next to it, i.e. \( n = 0 \) and \( n = 1 \).

**(a) Angular separation.**

The \( n^{\text{th}} \) bright fringe satisfies \( d\sin\theta = n\lambda \), so for the first maximum beside the central one (\( n = 1 \)):
\( \sin\theta = \dfrac{\lambda}{d} = \dfrac{\lambda}{100\lambda} = \dfrac{1}{100} = 0.01. \)
Because this is very small, \( \theta \approx \sin\theta \) in radians:
\( \theta = 0.01 \text{ rad}. \)
(Exactly, \( \theta = \sin^{-1}(0.01) = 0.0100002 \) rad, so the approximation is good to five significant figures.) The central maximum is at \( \theta = 0 \), so the angular separation between them is

**\( \theta = 0.01 \) rad** (about \( 0.573^\circ \)).

**(b) Distance between the two maxima on the screen.**

\( y = D\tan\theta \approx D\theta = 0.500 \times 0.01 = 5.00 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m} \)
\( y = 5.00 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m} = 0.5 \text{ cm} \)

**Answer:** (a) \( 0.01 \) rad;  (b) \( 0.5 \) cm \( = 5 \) mm.

This is of course just the fringe width \( W = \lambda D/d = D/100 \), which is why the wavelength itself is never needed.

**Given:** unpolarized light of intensity \( I_0 \); the first polaroid has its axis at \( 50^\circ \) to the **vertical**; the second polaroid has its axis **horizontal**.

**Step 1 -- through the first polaroid.** For unpolarized light the electric field takes every direction in the plane perpendicular to the propagation direction, and averaging \( \cos^2\phi \) over all of them gives \( 1/2 \). So whatever the orientation of the first polaroid,
\( I_1 = \dfrac{I_0}{2}. \)
The light emerging is now plane polarized along the axis of the first polaroid.

**Step 2 -- the angle between the two axes.** This is the step where care is needed, because the two axes are quoted from **different** reference directions. The first axis is \( 50^\circ \) from the vertical. The vertical and the horizontal are \( 90^\circ \) apart, so the first axis makes an angle
\( 90^\circ - 50^\circ = 40^\circ \)
with the **horizontal**. The second polaroid is horizontal, so the angle between the two polarizing axes is
\( \theta = 40^\circ. \)

**Step 3 -- Malus' law at the second polaroid.**
\( I_2 = I_1 \cos^2\theta = \dfrac{I_0}{2}\cos^2 40^\circ \)

**Answer:**
\( I_2 = \dfrac{I_0}{2}\left(\cos 40^\circ\right)^2 \)
Numerically, \( \cos 40^\circ = 0.7660 \), so \( \cos^2 40^\circ = 0.5868 \) and
\( I_2 = 0.5 \times 0.5868\, I_0 = 0.2934\, I_0, \)
i.e. about **29.3 % of the incident intensity**.

**Common error to avoid.** Using \( 50^\circ \) instead of \( 40^\circ \) would give \( 0.2066\,I_0 \). The angle in Malus' law is always the angle **between the two polarizing axes**, never the angle either axis makes with some external reference direction.

**Given:** biprism experiment. Distance from the slits (the two virtual sources) to the eyepiece, \( D = 1.2 \) m. Distance from the central bright band to the \( 20^{\text{th}} \) bright band \( = 0.4 \) cm. A convex lens is then placed between the biprism and the eyepiece, **90 cm from the eyepiece**, and the separation of the two magnified virtual images is \( 0.9 \) cm.

**Step 1 -- the fringe width.** The \( 20^{\text{th}} \) bright band is 20 fringe widths from the central one, so
\( W = \dfrac{0.4 \text{ cm}}{20} = 0.02 \text{ cm} = 2 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}. \)

**Step 2 -- the separation \( d \) of the two virtual sources.** This cannot be measured directly, which is why the lens is introduced. The lens forms a real, magnified image of the pair of virtual sources on the eyepiece. From the geometry:
\( \text{image distance } v = 90 \text{ cm} \quad (\text{lens to eyepiece}), \)
\( \text{object distance } u = 120 - 90 = 30 \text{ cm} \quad (\text{slits to lens}), \)
since the slits are \( 1.2 \) m \( = 120 \) cm from the eyepiece. Hence the magnification is
\( m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{90}{30} = 3. \)
The measured image separation is 3 times the true separation, so
\( d = \dfrac{0.9 \text{ cm}}{3} = 0.3 \text{ cm} = 3 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}. \)

**Step 3 -- the wavelength.** From \( W = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d} \),
\( \lambda = \dfrac{W d}{D} = \dfrac{\left(2 \times 10^{-4}\right)\left(3 \times 10^{-3}\right)}{1.2} = \dfrac{6 \times 10^{-7}}{1.2} = 5 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}. \)

**Answer:** \( \lambda = 5 \times 10^{-7} \) m \( = 5000 \) Å \( = 500 \) nm.

Here \( D \) is the **slit-to-screen** distance and \( d \) is the **separation of the two sources**; interchanging them is the commonest mistake in this calculation.

**Given:** Fraunhofer diffraction at a single slit. Screen distance \( D = 2 \) m; slit width \( a = 0.2 \) mm \( = 0.2 \times 10^{-3} \) m; the **first minimum** is at \( y = 5 \) mm \( = 5 \times 10^{-3} \) m on either side of the central maximum.

**Principle.** For single-slit diffraction the \( n^{\text{th}} \) **dark** fringe (minimum) satisfies
\( a \sin\theta = n\lambda. \)
Here \( n = 1 \). Since \( D \gg a \) the angle is small, so
\( \sin\theta \approx \tan\theta = \dfrac{y}{D}. \)

**Substituting.**
\( \sin\theta = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-3}}{2} = 2.5 \times 10^{-3} \)
\( \lambda = a \sin\theta = \left(0.2 \times 10^{-3}\right)\left(2.5 \times 10^{-3}\right) = 5 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} \)

**Answer:** \( \lambda = 5 \times 10^{-7} \) m \( = 5000 \) Å \( = 500 \) nm.

**Note the condition used.** For a **single slit** \( a\sin\theta = n\lambda \) gives a **dark** fringe. In two-slit interference the same expression \( d\sin\theta = n\lambda \) gives a **bright** one. Using the interference condition here would have given the wrong answer by a factor of 2.

**Given:** the intensity from one slit is twice that from the other, \( I_1 = 2 I_2 \).

**Principle.** Intensity is proportional to the square of the amplitude, so the amplitudes are
\( a_1 \propto \sqrt{I_1}, \qquad a_2 \propto \sqrt{I_2}. \)
At the centre of a **bright** fringe the two waves are in phase and the amplitudes **add**; at the centre of a **dark** fringe they are out of phase and the amplitudes **subtract**. Hence
\( I_{\max} \propto \left(a_1 + a_2\right)^2, \qquad I_{\min} \propto \left(a_1 - a_2\right)^2. \)

**Substituting.** Taking \( I_2 = I \) so that \( I_1 = 2I \), the amplitudes are in the ratio \( \sqrt{2} : 1 \). Therefore
\( \dfrac{I_{\max}}{I_{\min}} = \left(\dfrac{a_1 + a_2}{a_1 - a_2}\right)^{2} = \left(\dfrac{\sqrt{2} + 1}{\sqrt{2} - 1}\right)^{2}. \)
Rationalising the inner fraction,
\( \dfrac{\sqrt{2}+1}{\sqrt{2}-1} = \dfrac{\left(\sqrt{2}+1\right)^{2}}{\left(\sqrt{2}\right)^{2} - 1} = \dfrac{3 + 2\sqrt{2}}{1} = 3 + 2\sqrt{2}. \)
So
\( \dfrac{I_{\max}}{I_{\min}} = \left(3 + 2\sqrt{2}\right)^{2} = 17 + 12\sqrt{2}. \)
With \( \sqrt{2} = 1.41421 \):
\( \dfrac{I_{\max}}{I_{\min}} = 17 + 16.9706 = 33.97 \approx 34. \)

**Answer:** the intensities of the bright and dark fringes are in the approximate ratio \( \mathbf{34 : 1} \).

**Note.** The dark fringes are **not** completely dark here. That happens only when the two amplitudes are equal, which is condition 3 for a good interference pattern -- with unequal intensities the minima are proportional to \( (a_1 - a_2)^2 \neq 0 \) and the contrast is reduced.

**Given:** single slit. Wavelength \( \lambda = 550 \) nm \( = 550 \times 10^{-9} \) m; slit width \( a = 0.4 \) mm \( = 0.4 \times 10^{-3} \) m; screen distance \( D = 40 \) cm \( = 0.40 \) m.

**Principle.** The \( n^{\text{th}} \) **minimum** of a single-slit diffraction pattern lies at
\( y_{nd} = \dfrac{n \lambda D}{a}. \)
The two **first-order** minima are the ones with \( n = 1 \), one on each side of the central maximum, so the distance between them is
\( \Delta y = 2\,y_{1d} = \dfrac{2\lambda D}{a}. \)

**Substituting.**
\( y_{1d} = \dfrac{\left(550 \times 10^{-9}\right)\left(0.40\right)}{0.4 \times 10^{-3}} = \dfrac{2.2 \times 10^{-7}}{4 \times 10^{-4}} = 5.5 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m} \)
\( \Delta y = 2 \times 5.5 \times 10^{-4} = 1.1 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m} \)

**Answer:** the two first-order minima are \( 1.1 \times 10^{-3} \) m \( = \mathbf{1.1} \) **mm** apart.

**Note.** This distance is exactly the **width of the central bright fringe**, \( W_c = 2\lambda D/a \), since the central maximum is bounded by the first minimum on either side -- and it is twice the spacing \( W = \lambda D/a \) of the outer fringes.

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed answer is 1.274, which is exactly \( 4/\pi \) -- the value obtained by replacing \( \sin 45^\circ \) with \( 45^\circ \) expressed in radians (\( \pi/4 = 0.7854 \)). The small-angle approximation \( \sin\theta \approx \theta \) is not valid at \( 45^\circ \), where it is in error by about 11 %. The printed value is self-refuting: substituting \( a/\lambda = 1.274 \) back into the book's own condition \( a\sin\theta = \lambda \) gives \( \sin\theta = 0.7849 \), i.e. \( \theta = 51.7^\circ \), contradicting the \( 45.0^\circ \) stated in the question itself. The correct answer is \( 1/\sin 45^\circ = \sqrt{2} \approx 1.414 \), which back-solves to exactly \( 45.00^\circ \).]

**Given:** single slit, first diffraction **minimum** at \( \theta = 45.0^\circ \). Required: the ratio \( a/\lambda \) of slit width to wavelength.

**Principle.** For a single slit the \( n^{\text{th}} \) minimum satisfies
\( a \sin\theta = n\lambda. \)
For the **first** minimum, \( n = 1 \):
\( a \sin\theta = \lambda \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad \dfrac{a}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1}{\sin\theta}. \)

**Substituting \( \theta = 45.0^\circ \).**
\( \sin 45.0^\circ = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}} = 0.70711 \)
\( \dfrac{a}{\lambda} = \dfrac{1}{0.70711} = \sqrt{2} = 1.4142 \)

**Answer:** \( \dfrac{a}{\lambda} = \sqrt{2} \approx \mathbf{1.41} \).

**Check.** Substituting back, \( \sin\theta = \lambda/a = 1/1.4142 = 0.7071 \), giving \( \theta = 45.00^\circ \) exactly, as the question requires.

**Given:** single slit; screen distance \( D = 2.50 \) m; width of the **central maximum** \( W_c = 6.00 \) mm \( = 6.00 \times 10^{-3} \) m. Required: the slit width \( a \) for three different wavelengths.

**Principle.** The central bright fringe is spread between the first dark fringes on either side, so its width is twice the position of the first minimum:
\( W_c = 2\,y_{1d} = \dfrac{2\lambda D}{a} \qquad \Longrightarrow \qquad a = \dfrac{2\lambda D}{W_c}. \)
With \( D = 2.50 \) m and \( W_c = 6.00 \times 10^{-3} \) m the common factor is
\( \dfrac{2D}{W_c} = \dfrac{2 \times 2.50}{6.00 \times 10^{-3}} = 833.3\ \text{(dimensionless)}. \)

**(a) Visible light, \( \lambda = 500 \) nm \( = 5.00 \times 10^{-7} \) m.**
\( a = 833.3 \times 5.00 \times 10^{-7} = 4.167 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m} = \mathbf{0.4167 \text{ mm}} \)

**(b) Infrared, \( \lambda = 50\ \mu \)m \( = 5.00 \times 10^{-5} \) m.**
\( a = 833.3 \times 5.00 \times 10^{-5} = 4.167 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m} = \mathbf{41.67 \text{ mm}} \)

**(c) X-rays, \( \lambda = 0.500 \) nm \( = 5.00 \times 10^{-10} \) m.**
\( a = 833.3 \times 5.00 \times 10^{-10} = 4.167 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} = \mathbf{4.167 \times 10^{-4} \text{ mm}} \)

**Answer:** (a) \( 0.4167 \) mm,  (b) \( 41.67 \) mm,  (c) \( 4.167 \times 10^{-4} \) mm.

**What the three cases show.** Since \( a \propto \lambda \), each factor-of-100 change in wavelength changes the required slit width by the same factor. To spread an X-ray beam over the same 6 mm you would need a slit less than a micrometre across, whereas for infrared the "slit" is over 4 cm wide. This is exactly why diffraction is easy to see with long wavelengths and very hard to see with short ones -- **diffraction is noticeable only when the aperture is comparable with the wavelength.**

**Given:** wavelength \( \lambda = 5000 \) Å; diameter of the telescope objective \( D = 200 \) inch.

**Step 1 -- convert to SI units.** This is the step the question really tests.
\( \lambda = 5000 \) Å \( = 5000 \times 10^{-10} \text{ m} = 5 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m} \)
\( D = 200 \text{ inch} = 200 \times 2.54 \text{ cm} = 508 \text{ cm} = 5.08 \text{ m} \)
(using \( 1 \) inch \( = 2.54 \) cm.)

**Step 2 -- Rayleigh's criterion for a telescope.** The limit of resolution -- the smallest angular separation that can just be resolved -- is
\( \theta = \dfrac{1.22\,\lambda}{D}. \)

**Step 3 -- substitute.**
\( \theta = \dfrac{1.22 \times 5 \times 10^{-7}}{5.08} = \dfrac{6.1 \times 10^{-7}}{5.08} = 1.2008 \times 10^{-7} \text{ rad} \)

**Answer:** the limit of resolution is \( \theta \approx 1.2 \times 10^{-7} \) **rad** (about \( 0.025 \) arcsec).

**Note.** The question asks for the **limit of resolution**, which is the angle itself. Its reciprocal, \( R = 1/\theta = D/(1.22\lambda) \approx 8.3 \times 10^{6} \) per radian, is the **resolving power**. A larger objective gives a smaller \( \theta \) and hence a **better** (larger) resolving power, which is why large telescope apertures are worth their cost.

**Given:** biprism experiment. With \( \lambda_1 = 6000 \) Å the distance between two consecutive bright fringes is \( W_1 = 0.32 \) mm. The light is then changed to \( \lambda_2 = 4800 \) Å.

**Principle.** The distance between consecutive bright fringes is the fringe width
\( W = \dfrac{\lambda D}{d}. \)
The apparatus is unchanged, so \( D \) and \( d \) are the same in both cases and \( W \) is **directly proportional to \( \lambda \)**:
\( \dfrac{W_2}{W_1} = \dfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1}. \)

**Step 1 -- the new fringe width.**
\( W_2 = W_1 \times \dfrac{\lambda_2}{\lambda_1} = 0.32 \times \dfrac{4800}{6000} = 0.32 \times 0.8 = 0.256 \text{ mm} \)

**Step 2 -- the change.**
\( \Delta W = W_1 - W_2 = 0.32 - 0.256 = 0.064 \text{ mm} \)

**Answer:** the distance between consecutive bright fringes **decreases** by \( 0.064 \) mm (from \( 0.32 \) mm to \( 0.256 \) mm).

**Direction of the change.** The shorter wavelength gives the **smaller** fringe width, so the fringes move closer together. Stating only the magnitude \( 0.064 \) mm leaves the answer incomplete -- the question asks by how much the distance will *change*, and it is a decrease.
